links-notation 0.26.0 shipped on 2026-10-12 for every language ([releases](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation/releases)), but each lino-objects-codec package still pins a range that excludes it:

| Package | File | Constraint | Excludes 0.26.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| npm `lino-objects-codec` 0.9.2 | `js/package.json` | `"links-notation": "^0.25.2"` | yes (`^0.25` on a 0.x version is `>=0.25.2 <0.26.0`) |
| crates.io | `rust/Cargo.toml` | `links-notation = "0.25.2"` | yes (same caret rule) |
| PyPI | `python/pyproject.toml` | `links-notation>=0.25.2,<0.26.0` | yes |
| NuGet | `csharp/src/Lino.Objects.Codec/Lino.Objects.Codec.csproj` | `Link.Foundation.Links.Notation` `0.25.2` | resolves 0.25.2 |

## Reproduction

```console
$ npm init -y >/dev/null && npm i lino-objects-codec@0.9.2 links-notation@0.26.0
$ npm ls links-notation
+-- links-notation@0.26.0
`-- lino-objects-codec@0.9.2
  `-- links-notation@0.25.2
```

(Node 26.11.1, npm 11.20.0.) Any project that uses both packages gets two copies of the parser. links-notation's own `benchmarks/tools` resolves 0.25.2 through `lino-objects-codec`.

## Impact downstream

link-foundation/links-notation#348 updates every dependency in that repository to the latest release. This is one of the transitive entries it cannot move. The workaround is to leave it alone: `benchmarks/tools/package-lock.json` keeps 0.25.2 under `lino-objects-codec`, and the reason is recorded in link-foundation/links-notation#349.

## Suggested fix

Raise the constraint in all four languages to `0.26.0` (`^0.26.0`, `"0.26.0"`, `>=0.26.0,<0.27.0`, `Version="0.26.0"`), run the suites, and release. If 0.26.0 changes any parser behaviour the codec relies on, the readable-format fixtures in `fixtures/` should show it.
title: Update links-notation from 0.25.2 to 0.26.0 in all four packages

body:
## Summary

`formatIndented` writes a string value that contains a newline as a single-quoted reference spanning several lines, and `parseIndented` cannot read that output back.

## Reproduction (lino-objects-codec 0.9.3, links-notation 0.27.1, Node.js 26)

```js
import { formatIndented, parseIndented } from 'lino-objects-codec';

const text = formatIndented({ id: 'doc', obj: { t: 'line1\nline2' } });
console.log(JSON.stringify(text)); // "doc:\n  t 'line1\nline2'"
parseIndented({ text });           // throws: Unterminated quoted reference: t 'line1
```

A single-line value round-trips:

```js
parseIndented({ text: formatIndented({ id: 'doc', obj: { t: 'one line' } }) });
// { id: 'doc', obj: { t: 'one line' } }
```

## Expected

`parseIndented(formatIndented(x))` returns `x` for any string value. Either the formatter escapes or encodes the newline, or the indented parser accepts a quoted reference that continues on the next lines. `links-notation`'s `Parser` already accepts the same text (`"doc:\n  t 'line1\nline2'\n"` parses to a reference `line1\nline2`), and `encode`/`decode` round-trip multiline strings.

## Context

Found while building https://github.com/link-assistant/law, which stores its registry and catalog as indented Links Notation. That project works around it by keeping catalog values single-line (error messages are collapsed to one line) and using `encode`/`decode` for anything multiline.
title: parseIndented cannot read formatIndented output for multiline string values

body:
## Summary

Every dependency of this repository should be at its latest release (the maintainers' standing requirement, applied first in link-assistant/formal-ai#1169). The latest published `lino-objects-codec` (0.7.0) and `rust/Cargo.toml` on `main` (checked 2026-09-29) declare dependencies whose latest release is outside the declared range:

| Dependency | Declared | Latest release |
|---|---|---|
| `links-notation` | 0.16.1 | 0.22.0 |

Consumers such as link-assistant/formal-ai compile a second copy of these crates next to the current ones, and cannot move to current versions of shared types.

## Requirements

1. R1: update every dependency in the table to its latest release and adapt the code to the new APIs (list each breaking change handled in the pull request description).
2. R2: run `cargo update` so the lockfile has no semver-compatible update pending (`cargo update --dry-run` prints no `Updating` lines).
3. R3: add a CI job that fails when a direct dependency is behind its latest release, unless the manifest line carries a comment with an open issue URL explaining the blocker. A ready-made form: `cargo install cargo-outdated --locked && cargo outdated --root-deps-only --exit-code 1` (for JavaScript packages in this repository: `npm outdated` exits 1 when anything is outdated).
4. R4: publish a release containing the updates (crates.io and npm where applicable).

## How to test

`cargo outdated --root-deps-only --exit-code 1` exits 0; `cargo tree -d` in a fresh crate that depends on this release and on the latest versions of the crates in the table shows no duplicates for them.
title: Update links-notation to the latest release (0.16.1->0.22.0) and enforce dependency freshness in CI

body:
Actual consumer failure with lino-objects-codec0.9.0 and Node22.23.0, while verifying a full saved Lazada associative case. The codec successfully emitted valid readable Links Notation, but cannot read it back.

The discovery-publication-source document contains1,764 historical proof records,144,497,741 UTF8 bytes, content SHA25633288f6b43e93e619e92eb622383da322ba8bb6022503dc6e8faa6f9c5a088a4 (gzip24,975,140 bytes). A smaller56,510,065-byte cache notation is also present. Source JSON, compressed/uncompressed hashes and binary frames remain intact.

Actual stack:
```
RangeError: Invalid array length
 at Function.from (<anonymous>)
 at tokenize (.../lino-objects-codec/src/readable.js:582:23)
 at Module.decode (.../src/readable.js:224:18)
 at ObjectCodec.decode (.../src/codec.js:200:21)
 at decode (.../src/codec.js:784:24)
```

`tokenize` calls `Array.from(text)` before scanning, multiplying memory use and reaching V8 backing-array limits for a valid large document. A narrow consumer workaround uses direct string indexing and string slices instead of the character array and corresponding slice/join calls. ASCII delimiters and complete Unicode text/quote runs must round-trip. The separate escaped-payload decoder also materializes arrays and deserves bounded Unicode/UTF8 processing for giant single values.

Please support decoding valid large documents without whole-document character arrays, preserve exact encoded/decoded JSON and Unicode/quote/escaped-marker behavior, and add a realistic regression. The consumer will keep verifying every saved notation record against JSON and binary conversion, not skip decode or remove history. A public fixed/failed archive receipt and consumer workaround link will follow after full validation and commit. No marketplace requests are needed to reproduce.
title: Readable decoder fails on valid 144MB document: tokenize materializes Array.from(text)

Versions resolved from the registries today.

## C# — `csharp/`

Four implementations, four parser versions. The shared fixtures verify that the four codecs agree with each other, but not that they agree about the *grammar underneath*, so this spread is invisible to the conformance suites. link-foundation/links-notation#288 is a live example: whatever is decided about the empty reference lands in a parser release, and today the four would adopt it at four different times. ## Suggested checks

- the shared fixtures still pass in all four languages after the bumps;
- a document written by each implementation reads back identically in the other three;
- the major-version bumps are separate commits, so a regression is bisectable.
title: Update all dependencies in all four languages: major versions behind in each, and four different links-notation pins

body:
Thank you for #43 — `encode_line`/`decode_line` in 0.5.0 solve the framing and the pair/array ambiguity cleanly, and the `(o: …)` marker is a better answer than the `:` prefix a downstream project (link-assistant/router) had invented. Verified against `links-notation` 0.14.0: every case round-trips and parses, including the 2-element-scalar-first array, empty keys, and the empty object/array distinction.

One property from #43 does not hold in practice, and it is the one the request was for.

## What happens

`format_string` (`readable.rs:264`) routes through `needs_encoding`, which is true for **any control character**:

```rust
fn needs_encoding(value: &str) -> bool {
    value.chars().any(char::is_control)
}
```

A newline is a control character, so any string containing one becomes `(base64 "…")`:

```rust
let body = "You are a helpful assistant.\nModel: claude-opus-5\nBe concise.";
encode_line(&record)
// (o: (phase "client_request") (model "claude-opus-5")
//     (body (base64 "WW91IGFyZSBhIGhlbHBmdWwgYXNzaXN0YW50LgpNb2RlbDog…")))

line.contains("claude-opus-5")     // true  — a short top-level field
line.contains("helpful assistant") // false — anything inside a body
```

## Why this is the case that matters

The module doc says the single-line form exists so "an append-only log stays greppable" (`readable.rs:44`). Measured against a real 400-record production request log:

| | count | share |
|---|---|---|
| strings | 54,739 | |
| containing a newline → base64 | 3,824 | **7.0%** |
| **string bytes** in those | 8,309,499 of 11,841,273 | **70.2%** |

So 7% of strings, but **70% of the text**. Multi-line strings are not an edge case in a log of HTTP exchanges — they are the request bodies, response bodies and system prompts, which is precisely what an operator greps. The short fields that stay readable are the ones already visible in a summary.

This is the same outcome `encode_compact` was avoided for, arrived at by a narrower path.

## Why escaping rather than base64 works here

A newline genuinely must not reach the output — it would end the record. But it can be *escaped* rather than *encoded*, keeping the rest of the string readable. The downstream project percent-escapes the four characters that can break framing or tokenising, leaving everything else literal:

```
(o: (body "You are a helpful assistant.%0AModel: claude-opus-5%0ABe concise."))
```

`grep "helpful assistant"` finds that; `grep "claude-opus-5"` finds it inside the body too.

Fuzzed over 6,000 values against both libraries, escaping `%` `"` `(` `)` `\` and the control characters: **0 parse failures, 0 decode failures, 0 round-trip failures, 0 multi-line records**. Notably the codec-native doubled-quote form failed 241 of the same 6,000 (it desynchronises `parse_lino` once siblings follow), so the escape set does need care — but it is achievable.

## What I would suggest

Restrict base64 to what actually cannot be represented, and escape what can:

- escape `\n`, `\r`, `\t` (and the escape introducer itself) inline;
- keep `(base64 "…")` for genuinely unrepresentable content — other control characters, lone surrogates, invalid UTF-8;
- or, if the escape syntax is a larger decision, expose the choice (`encode_line_escaped`, or a codec option) so a log can opt into readability.

Happy to open a PR if the direction is agreeable — the downstream implementation and its fuzz harness already exist and I can port them.

## Note

Found while adopting 0.5.0 downstream to replace exactly the private dialect #43 was filed about. The adoption is otherwise a straight win; this is the one property that would regress a log that #328 (downstream) had already made readable.
title: encode_line base64-encodes any string with a newline, so 70% of a real log's text stops being greppable

body:
## Summary

`encode()` base64-encodes every string and emits the whole object on one line. The result is not human-readable, which defeats the point of Links Notation as "the portable, human-readable syntax" and "the reviewable import/export projection".

Requested: make an indented, plain-text form the default, and keep the current single-line encoded form available under an explicit name.

## What is produced today

Real stored file from a deployment that persists its state through this crate:

```
(object ((str dHlwZQ==) (str Um91dGVyU3RhdGU=)) ((str c3VidHlwZQ==) (str VG9rZW5TdG9yZQ==)) ((str dm…
```

Decoding by hand: `dHlwZQ==` → `type`, `Um91dGVyU3RhdGU=` → `RouterState`, `c3VidHlwZQ==` → `subtype`, `VG9rZW5TdG9yZQ==` → `TokenStore`.

The structure is sensible, but nobody can see that without running base64 on every field. Reviewing a diff, grepping for a key, or spotting a wrong value are all impossible.

Encoding is unconditional (`src/lib.rs:33`), so ASCII keys like `type` need it as much as text that actually does. `src/lib.rs:14` states the reason:

> **UTF-8 Support**: Full Unicode string support using base64 encoding

Unicode support is a real requirement, but the notation already has a quoting strategy for it, and this crate implements it in `format_indented_value` — single quotes, double quotes, and doubling for embedded quotes.

## The proposed default

One construct — `( )` — for both objects and arrays, at every level including the root. Indentation is for readability only; what distinguishes the two is the content: `key value` pairs make an object, bare values make an array.

**JSON:**

```json
{
  "type": "RouterState",
  "server": { "host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 18878 },
  "models": ["claude-haiku", "claude-opus"],
  "value": [
    { "id": "7cf7abf6", "label": "bootstrap-admin", "ttl_hours": 24, "revoked": false },
    { "id": "94b36f7e", "label": "wrapper-run", "ttl_hours": 720, "revoked": false }
  ]
}
```

**Links Notation:**

```
(
  type "RouterState"
  server (
    host "127.0.0.1"
    port 18878
  )
  models (
    "claude-haiku"
    "claude-opus"
  )
  value (
    (
      id "7cf7abf6"
      label "bootstrap-admin"
      ttl_hours 24
      revoked false
    )
    (
      id "94b36f7e"
      label "wrapper-run"
      ttl_hours 720
      revoked false
    )
  )
)
```

### Mapping

| JSON | Links Notation |
|---|---|
| object, including the root | `( )` containing `key value` pairs, one per line |
| array | `( )` containing values, one per line |
| object as an array element | its own `( )` |
| string | double quotes, no encoding |
| number, `true`/`false`, `null` | bare, so the type survives the round trip |

### Why parentheses rather than indentation alone for a nested object

Both parse, but they mean different things. Verified against the parser:

```
server
  host "127.0.0.1"
  port 18878
```
→ `(server (host …))`, `(server (port …))` — two separate facts about `server`.

```
server (
  host "127.0.0.1"
  port 18878
)
```
→ `server → [(host …), (port …)]` — one object with two fields, which is what the JSON meant.

The same argument applies to array elements: without their own `( )`, the fields of consecutive records merge into one flat list and the record boundaries cannot be recovered.

## Dependency

This form relies on parentheses opening a nested indentation context, which landed in [link-foundation/links-notation#283](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation/pull/283) and is released as `links-notation` **0.14.0**.

This crate currently depends on `links-notation` 0.13, where the behaviour is absent: inside `( )`, indentation is ignored and every line collapses into one flat list. So **the dependency has to be raised to 0.14 before the new default can work**.

Verified against the 0.14 parser: the document above parses into exactly the structure described, and

```
value (
  id "1"
  label "one"
)
```

now yields two links — `(id "1")` and `(label "one")` — where 0.13 produced four loose references.

## What is being asked

1. Raise the `links-notation` dependency to 0.14, so parentheses open a nested indentation context.
2. Make the indented, plain-text form above the **default** output of `encode()`.
3. Keep the current single-line base64 form as a configurable option under an explicit name — `encode_compact()` or `encode_obfuscated()` — so the code and its tests are preserved and callers opt into it deliberately. Any other output styles stay available the same way: configurable, never the default.
4. Encode a value only when it genuinely cannot be represented as text, and mark those values individually rather than encoding everything.
5. Accept both forms when decoding, so existing files keep working and migrate on next write.
6. Update the docs: `src/lib.rs:866` currently teaches the opposite — `// String "Alice" is base64-encoded as "QWxpY2U="`.

The point is the default. A library called without reading its documentation should produce a readable file; today the readable form exists but is reachable only by knowing about a separate module.

## Tests worth adding

- `encode()` of an object with ASCII keys and values produces output containing them verbatim;
- output spans multiple lines with indentation, not one line;
- nested objects and arrays round-trip to the same structure;
- an object used as an array element keeps its boundary;
- numbers and booleans survive the round trip as numbers and booleans, not strings;
- a value containing quotes, newlines or non-ASCII text round-trips exactly;
- a value that cannot be represented as text is marked individually and round-trips;
- a file written in the previous base64 form still decodes.

## Note

Found while auditing what a downstream project stores on disk. Every fact needed to read the file was present, but only after base64-decoding four fields by hand to discover the structure was correct all along.
title: encode() base64-encodes every string on one line, so .lino files are not human-readable — the readable formatter already exists but is not the default

body:
## Problem

`lino-objects-codec@0.3.6` currently documents and exports the typed object codec as the primary `encode/decode` path. The generated notation preserves JavaScript types, but it is much harder to review because it emits markers such as `object`, `str`, `int`, and base64 strings.

For reviewable repository data files, an untyped/dynamic recursive object mode is needed as the default documented path, with the typed codec still available when exact JavaScript type preservation is required.

Expected readable shape:

```lino
obj_root:
  title `Indian Law`
  defaultLanguage en
  maxLines 1500
  sourceMetadata obj_root_source_metadata
  languages obj_root_languages

obj_root_source_metadata:
  generatedFrom obj_root_source_metadata_generated_from
  lastVerified 2026-05-10
```

## Reproduction

```js
import { encode, jsonToLino, linoToJson, formatIndented } from "lino-objects-codec";

const data = {
  title: "Indian Law",
  defaultLanguage: "en",
  maxLines: 1500,
  nested: { ok: true },
  items: ["a", 1]
};

console.log(encode({ obj: data }));
console.log(jsonToLino({ json: data }));
console.log(linoToJson({ lino: jsonToLino({ json: data }) }));
console.log(formatIndented({ id: "obj_root", obj: data }));
```

Observed with `0.3.6`:

```lino
(object ((str dGl0bGU=) (str SW5kaWFuIExhdw==)) ((str ZGVmYXVsdExhbmd1YWdl) (str ZW4=)) ((str bWF4TGluZXM=) (int 1500)) ((str bmVzdGVk) (object ((str b2s=) (bool true)))) ((str aXRlbXM=) (array (str YQ==) (int 1))))
```

`jsonToLino` provides compact untyped dynamic notation and `linoToJson` parses it back, which is useful. However:

- the README quick start still favors the typed/base64 object codec;
- `formatIndented` is flat-only and converts nested objects/arrays to strings such as `[object Object]` and `a,1`;
- there is no out-of-the-box recursive indented untyped writer/parser matching the reviewable form above.

## Workaround

Projects can implement a local recursive writer/parser on top of `links-notation`, or use `jsonToLino/linoToJson` when compact one-line-ish notation is acceptable.

## Suggested Fix

- Add a recursive untyped dynamic object codec for human-readable repository data.
- Make the README and examples favor that readable dynamic mode by default.
- Keep the current typed `encode/decode` API available and documented for exact type-preserving serialization, circular references, and object identity.
- Extend `formatIndented`/`parseIndented`, or add new named functions, so nested objects and arrays can round-trip without `[object Object]` stringification.

This would let data catalogs use readable Links Notation by default while still preserving the typed codec for cases that need it.
title: Support readable untyped recursive object encoding as the default documented mode

body:
## Summary

The lino-objects-codec library should support an indented Links Notation format for output, in addition to the current parentheses-based format.

## Requested Format

The library should support formatting objects in an indented style like:

```
6dcf4c1b-ff3f-482c-95ab-711ea7d1b019
  uuid "6dcf4c1b-ff3f-482c-95ab-711ea7d1b019"
  status "executed"
  command "echo test"
  exitCode "0"
```

Where the first line is the object identifier (UUID), and subsequent lines are indented properties in the format:
```
  <key> "<value>"
```

## Current Format

Currently, the library only supports the parentheses-based format:
```
(type value)
(object (str key) (str value))
```

## Use Case

This indented format is requested for displaying execution status in a more human-readable way while maintaining the Links Notation style.

## Reference

Related to PR link-foundation/start#47 - Add --status --output-format support

---
Filed from PR link-foundation/start#47 per user feedback.
title: Add indented Links Notation format support to lino-objects-codec

For example:

```js
const obj = {
  "self": obj
  "other": { "1": 1, "2": 2 }
};
```

Self reference should be translated as (or similar):

```
(obj: 
  (self obj)
  (other (
     (1 1)
     (2 2)
   ))
)
```

to links notation

How to read links notation:

```
(self-reference: first-reference second-reference ...)
```

Implement new style in both JS and Python versions.
title: Instead of `ref` reference/marker use built-in references in links notation

We need to create simplies possible prototype for universal serializer/deserialer for Links Notation

We should use python library from https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation for that.

Links Notation is based on references and links, so it should be possible to easily serialize/deserialize objects with circular references and more.

But at first we need to focus on the most common object types (like JSON like objects in Python).

We should use TDD and start with tests suite, make it fail, and implement failing tests.
title: Python Object Serde prototype
